body: Pulmonary embolism is far more likely to cause acute hypoxia than it is to cause acute hypercapnia. Across gas-exchange studies, hypocapnia occurs in roughly 74% of PE patients and hypoxemia/elevated A–a gradient in ~80%. Despite increased physiologic dead space, compensatory hyperventilation keeps CO₂ low in all but the most extensive emboli. A good rule of thumb is that pulmonary embolism patients are hypocapnic.

The lining of the gut is dynamic. It turns over constantly, and what drives that turnover is food in the lumen. Take the food away and the mucosa thins out. The barrier starts to leak. And soon after, the flora of the GI tract are able to translocate into the peritoneal cavity.

Severe pancreatitis makes the point well. Patients fed through a tube get fewer infections and less multi-organ failure than patients fed by vein. Bedside experience says so, and so does a good body of research. Nutrients in the bowel do more than supply calories. They keep the wall intact.

Feed the gut early, within 24 to 48 hours, once the patient is hemodynamically stable, because an unused gut becomes a leaky one.

A practice update for some: the American Gastroenterological Association recommends abandoning the traditional *nil per os* "pancreatic rest" approach of old in pancreatitis in favor of early feeding (generally within 24 hours) in those patients who can (N/V, obstruction, or ileus might be reasons they cannot).

Every sailboat has a “no-go zone,” roughly 45 degrees on either side of the wind. Turn into it and the sails lose their drive. The boat slows, stops, and can no longer steer. Sailors call this being “in irons,” after the shackles once used to chain prisoners.

There are ways to escape, but none are fast. For the great warships of the age of sail, the stakes were high. A ship that failed to tack was said to have “missed stays.” Near rocks or in a storm, that could wreck her. In battle, it could leave her stern exposed to a raking broadside. Crews that tacked cleanly held a real advantage, and navies drilled sail handling relentlessly for that reason.

Every sailor has a favorite point of sail. Mine is close-hauled. It means sailing as close to the wind as the boat allows, right at the edge of the no-go zone.

A normal CO₂ in a struggling asthmatic should scare you.

During an acute exacerbation, patients breathe fast and blow off CO₂. The gas you expect is a low PaCO₂ and a respiratory alkalosis. So when someone is working hard, tachypneic, and the gas comes back “normal,” that is not reassurance. It means ventilation is falling off. The respiratory muscles are tiring, and failure is coming.

A frankly high and climbing PaCO₂ with acidosis means you are already there, or nearly so.

Read the number against the patient in front of you. Normal is only normal in context.

At the end of diastole, atrial contraction tops off the ventricles. This “atrial kick” supplies about 20–30% of filling, and more in stiff ventricles. In AF the atria quiver instead of contracting, so the kick is gone. Add RVR and diastole shortens too: less filling time, no top-off, and stroke volume drops. The coronaries also fill in diastole, so demand ischemia can follow.

Pearl: before slowing the rate, ask whether the tachycardia is the problem or the compensation. In sepsis or bleeding, it may be what’s holding the pressure up.

Today I read about analgosedation, the practice of treating pain before reaching for a sedative in ventilated patients. It’s a conditional recommendation in the 2018 PADIS guidelines. Protocols built around it have shown less sedative use, shorter ventilation, and shorter ICU stays.

The point I want to remember is that sedation and analgesia aren’t interchangeable. A patient who looks agitated may be in pain, and propofol won’t fix that.

Arterial blood gas during wakefulness to document hypercapnia (PaCO₂ ≥ 45 mm Hg) is the gold standard and the one indispensable step in the diagnosis of obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) as OHS cannot be diagnosed without demonstrating daytime hypercapnia.

A patient started on norepinephrine for a soft MAP put out 5 L of urine over the next day with no furosemide. That’s pressure natriuresis.

When renal perfusion pressure rises, the kidney excretes more sodium and water, and the response is steep: a small gain in MAP produces a large gain in output. Medullary flow and interstitial pressure go up, and proximal NHE3 moves away from the apical membrane, so less sodium is reabsorbed. He was volume overloaded but underperfused, which put him on the flat part of the curve. The pressor moved him onto the steep part, and the kidney cleared what it couldn’t before.

Lesson: oliguria in a hypotensive, overloaded patient may be a pressure problem rather than a diuretic problem. Fix the MAP first, then reassess. After that, follow lytes and volume closely, because the kidney won’t stop at euvolemia on its own.

The drug follows the clot, and the clot follows the flow.

Arterial clots form under high flow and shear, usually on a ruptured plaque. Platelets stick and aggregate first, making a pale “white clot.” Venous clots form where blood is slow or still. There the coagulation cascade dominates, and fibrin traps red cells into a “red clot.”

So antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor) are for arterial disease: MI, ischemic stroke, stent thrombosis. Anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin, DOACs) are for venous disease: DVT and PE.

AFib is the exception that proves the rule. The clot forms in a stagnant left atrial appendage. It is on the arterial side but follows venous physics. That’s why we anticoagulate rather than give aspirin, even though the outcome we fear is a stroke.

**SBT Readiness screen (all should be met):**

1. Cause improving: whatever led to intubation is resolving or resolved.
2. Oxygenation: FiO₂ ≤ 0.4–0.5, PEEP ≤ 5–8, SpO₂ ≥ 88–90% (or P/F ≥ 150–200).
3. Hemodynamics: stable with no or low-dose, stable pressors. No active ischemia, and HR ≤ 140.
4. Respiratory drive: initiating spontaneous breaths.
5. Neuro: arousable after SAT (RASS roughly −1 to +1), ideally following commands.
6. Labs/other: pH ≥ 7.25, no major uncorrected electrolyte problems, afebrile or near it, Hgb ≥ 7.
7. No planned procedures requiring sedation or the airway soon.

When pressors aren’t working, think micronutrients

Thiamine. Shoshin beriberi causes vasodilatory shock with rising lactate. Suspect it with alcohol use, bariatric surgery, TPN, or loop diuretics. Give IV thiamine empirically rather than waiting for a level.

Ionized calcium. Low iCa reduces vascular tone and contractility. Check Mg too, because hypomagnesemia drives hypocalcemia.

Selenium. Consider it in dialysis, long-term TPN, or malabsorption.

In chronic orthostatic hypotension, B12 deficiency (confirmed with MMA) causes autonomic dysfunction. Iron deficiency and low vitamin D have weaker associations.
